# How to Set a Domain Name with php artisan serve

When you transition from a local development environment like WAMP to Laravel's built-in server, the ability to bind specific domain names becomes less intuitive. In WAMP, you manually configure `httpd.conf` or virtual host files to map a document root to a specific hostname and port. With `php artisan serve`, the default behavior is to listen on `127.0.0.1` at port `8000`, ignoring any custom domain name passed in `.env` files. This isn't because Laravel ignores your configuration, but because the development server is designed for rapid iteration rather than production-like routing.

You cannot simply add a line to your `.env` file and expect `php artisan serve --domain=blog.local` to work out of the box. The underlying PHP SAPI (Server API) used by `artisan serve` does not support binding to specific hostnames in the same way Apache or Nginx do. When you attempt to run a command like `php artisan serve --host=blog.local`, you will encounter an error because the server strictly limits its listening interface to IPv4 loopback (`127.0.0.1`) or all interfaces (`0.0.0.0`), but it does not parse hostname headers from the URL scheme to determine the binding address.

To effectively use a custom domain name with the Laravel development server, you must rely on browser-level resolution rather than server-level configuration. The most straightforward approach is to modify your system's `hosts` file. On Windows, this is located at `C:\Windows\System32\drivers\etc\hosts`. You can add an entry mapping your desired domain to the loopback address:

```text
127.0.0.1 blog.local
```

Once this mapping exists, you can run the server with a custom port (which you do have control over):

```bash
php artisan serve --port=8001
```

When you navigate to `http://blog.local:8001` in your browser, the operating system resolves `blog.local` to `127.0.0.1`, allowing the request to reach the Laravel application. This method decouples the URL structure from the network binding, effectively simulating a domain name without requiring changes to the PHP runtime or Apache configuration.

### Understanding the Host Binding Limitation

The fundamental difference between hosting with `php artisan serve` and WAMP lies in how they handle the HTTP protocol stack. WAMP utilizes Apache (or Nginx), which listens on specific ports and can be configured via virtual hosts to accept connections based on the `Host` header sent by the client. Apache then routes that request to the correct document root and loads the appropriate configuration files.

In contrast, `php artisan serve` is a lightweight CLI tool built using PHP's built-in web server functions. It prioritizes simplicity and speed over feature parity with production servers. Because it does not parse virtual host configurations or manage SSL certificates for multiple domains out of the box, it lacks the flexibility to bind directly to a hostname like `blog.local`.

This architectural difference creates a specific pitfall for developers trying to test multi-domain setups locally. If you attempt to run two instances of `php artisan serve` simultaneouslyâone for `site1.com` and one for `site2.com`âyou cannot distinguish them by domain name if both are bound to the same IP. You would be forced to use different ports, which defeats the purpose of having multiple domains. With a virtual host setup (like WAMP or a production Nginx stack), you could run a single server listening on port 80 and route requests based on the `Host` header.

### When to Use Which Approach

The choice between using `php artisan serve` and a full hosting environment like WAMP often comes down to your current development workflow. `php artisan serve` is excellent for testing a single application quickly without installing a web server stack, managing Apache configurations, or dealing with permission issues on the document root. It ensures that you are running exactly the code intended for development, isolated from other site configurations.

However, if your goal is to test multi-domain routing, shared hosting environments, or SSL certificate handling (using tools like `php artisan serve --ssl`), the limitations of the CLI server become apparent. In those cases, configuring a virtual host in WAMP or setting up Nginx/Apache on a VPS provides a more production-replica environment where you can specify document roots, server names, and ports in a single configuration file.

If you are struggling with domain resolution issues while developing, remember that the `hosts` file is the universal solution for local development regardless of the web server technology. It allows you to define your own DNS records locally without polluting the public internet.
